title: Mecca, in the Vars
hookLine: Bhai Gurdas tells how Nanak answered the qazis that deeds, not labels, count (Bhai Gurdas, Var 1)

lines: OPEN YOUR BOOK AND TELL US.
A TRAVELER IN BLUE, WITH A BOOK.
cards: Open your book, and tell us. In Bhai Gurdas's first var, that's the demand put to Guru Nanak at Mecca. A traveler in blue clothes, with a staff in his hand and a book under his arm, has arrived among the pilgrims.
Year one told one story from that visit: the traveler asleep with his feet toward the Kaaba. Today, Bhai Gurdas's next stanza, and the question that came after. Today's word: Mecca.

teach.h: WHO IS GREATER, HINDU OR MUSLIM?
teach.b: In Bhai Gurdas's telling, the qazis and mullahs gather around Nanak with the question of the age you heard about three days ago. Open your book, they say, and tell us: who is greater, the Hindu or the Muslim?
It's a trap shaped like a quiz. Pick one, and you've joined the quarrel. Refuse, and you look evasive.

teach.h: WITHOUT GOOD DEEDS, BOTH WILL WEEP.
teach.b: Bhai Gurdas says Nanak answered the pilgrims plainly: without good deeds, both will weep. Neither the Hindu nor the Muslim, by the label alone, finds shelter at God's court.
Then he reaches for a picture from the dyer's yard. Safflower gives cloth a bright color, but it's a raw color. Wash it, and it runs out.

teach.h: SAFFLOWER DYE: GONE IN THE WASH.
teach.b: A label, Bhai Gurdas suggests, is like that dye: bright on the surface, gone in the first wash. What holds is what's done. Look at what Nanak doesn't do here.
He doesn't say both are wrong, or both are right, or that some third thing is better. He moves the question off the label and onto the life. Deeds; amal is the word Bhai Gurdas uses.
And he names the real problem in the same stanza: people quarrel with each other while Ram and Rahim are one.
For Sikhs, the weight of this answer is that it falls on everyone equally.
A Sikh who leans on the label of being a Sikh is wearing the same safflower dye. The book Nanak opens, in this telling, doesn't announce a winner. It asks what you did.

how: Sikhs retell Guru Nanak's answer at Mecca, as Bhai Gurdas gives it, as a teaching that good deeds, not religious labels, count before God, and they apply it to themselves as much as to anyone.

o: where Nanak said that without good deeds both will weep
where Nanak's first hymn was written into the Granth
where Nanak was made a qazi and stayed to teach

games.q: inside the stanza — tap the pairs.

s: in Bhai Gurdas's telling, Nanak names the Muslim greater
he names neither. without good deeds, both will weep.
in the telling, Nanak says a third label is better than both
he moves the question off labels altogether and onto deeds.
the safflower picture is about a color that doesn't last
bright on the surface, gone in the wash, like a label without deeds.

games.q: you're a traveler at Mecca. the scholars gather and say: open your book and tell us, who is greater, the Hindu or the Muslim?
o: say both are wrong and offer a third answer.
say that without good deeds, both will weep.
games.why: in Bhai Gurdas's telling, Nanak refuses the contest: no label alone finds shelter at God's court. what holds is what's done.

practice: Choose one good deed nobody will trace back to you: paying for the next person's coffee, wiping down the shared table at work, picking up the litter on your own street.
Decide what it will be, then let it go, with no post and no telling anyone, not even later. If you pray, you can offer the deed quietly in the Name.

wordCard.voice: Mecca, in the vars. In Bhai Gurdas's telling, the place where Nanak was asked who is greater, and answered that without good deeds, both will weep.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi: deeds. It's the word Bhai Gurdas uses in Nanak's answer about good deeds.

carryVoice: Your line: deeds, not labels. A book opened, and no winner announced. Day seven hundred two, done.

sources.ref: Vaaran Bhai Gurdas, Var 1, pauri 32 (Nanak at Mecca)
